steering_ledger.verbatim: "So \"no sound thread-attribution method exists here\" is refutable: for Codex the parent->child edge is explicit, and for Claude the sidechain grouping is present. What's actually missing is narrower than R-17 concluded - a collector, a bus<->transcript join key, an outcome label, and a Task/SubagentStop hook (none of the 13 registered hooks in .claude/settings.json matches Task)." - this sounds eerily similar to the coordinator-agent skill I just refactored with claude today. "One caveat I won't let slide: the orchestrator repo's concurrency work (src/runtime/concurrency.py, NUMA quarters, placement veto) is inference concurrency - model instances on hardware. It is a completely disjoint axis from agent fan-out, shares no code or metric, and conflating the two would be a category error." - true there is a subtle difference between PARL and what's possible on our hardware. First, our model currently have relatively small context windows (~260k), this means that on large fan out, the individual batch threads have a lot less context to work with. This may not be an issue if fan-out tasks are narrowly scoped but typically when claude fans out, the subagents easily accumulate ~100k token contexts. We still don't know how much the REPL allows us to avoid such large contexts. As such, the max number of fanout agents on our models is quite reduce at the moment (-np 2 on full CPU instance, and -np 8 on the GPU architect_general). Secondly, the fanout doesn't necessarily mean fast execution. If the largest most expensive models guides the fanout, the individual threads will be slow on our system. This is precisely why our orchestration stack was built with the worker_general role available. This model is supposed to take narrowly scoped tasks and execute them fast. The intelligent model thus decides the fan out but the actual fanout threads aren't limited by the bandwidth-per-token required to operate the more intelligent model. We do allow the router to tap into the batched processes and this, if tied holistically intop the orhcestrator's task decomposition and distribution shoudl allow importing some of the power of the batching used in PARL to our wheelhouse. Ultimately, the task decomposition is the crux if I'm nto mistaken
steering_ledger.effect_on_stage1: Establishes the EPYC-native framing: the relevant plane is orchestrator TASK DECOMPOSITION mapping onto np batching, not Claude agent fan-out; worker_general is the structural analogue of PARL frozen subagents. Recorded in intake-1106 notes as a structural note. Also flagged a duplicate-work check against today's coordinator-agent skill refactor — CHECKED, no overlap: commits 2f787163/22c4aff5/d5c0848c/c436d5be encode DOCTRINE, and grep of the skill for parent_thread_id/isSidechain/promptId/critical-path returns zero hits.

steering_ledger.verbatim: "- Context is the real binding constraint, and it's the one nobody's reward function models. ~260k window against subagents that routinely accumulate ~100k means fan-out width and per-thread context trade off directly against KV. PARL's step-count formulation is blind to this - CriticalSteps counts steps, not tokens or KV residency, and it assumes uniform step cost." - dont' forget that we try avoiding large contexts by leveraging the REPL. This is a key element to take into consideration
steering_ledger.effect_on_stage1: Corrects the main's overstatement: context binds only ABSENT the REPL. REPL keeps child reasoning out of the parent context (cf. intake-536 RAO automatic context isolation, rao-redel-substrate-spike.md, repl-turn-efficiency.md), so it is the lever that breaks the fan-out-width vs per-thread-context tradeoff. Recorded against intake-1109, whose positive prediction is that fan-out wins only when single-agent context utilization binds.
